## What it is

Eclipse Mosquitto is a small open-source MQTT broker (MQTT 5.0, 3.1.1 and 3.1). Sensors, Zigbee2MQTT, Home Assistant, Node-RED and scripts publish messages to *topics* on it and subscribe to the topics they care about, so devices on the home network can talk to each other without knowing about each other ([mosquitto.org](https://mosquitto.org), [README](https://github.com/eclipse-mosquitto/mosquitto/blob/v2.1.2/README.md)). It has no web UI in this package: clients connect over MQTT on port **1883**.

**Licence:** `EPL-2.0 OR BSD-3-Clause`, dual-licensed under the Eclipse Public License 2.0 or the Eclipse Distribution License 1.0, which is BSD-3-Clause ([LICENSE.txt at v2.1.2](https://github.com/eclipse-mosquitto/mosquitto/blob/v2.1.2/LICENSE.txt)). The image's `org.opencontainers.image.licenses` label gives the same expression. GitHub reports `NOASSERTION` for the repository, so the licence gate confirms the licence from the research licence matrix (`research-output/evidence/license-matrix.csv`, row "Eclipse Mosquitto (default MQTT 5 app, W8-R1)"). That row used to say `EPL-2.0 OR EDL-1.0 (BSD-3-Clause)`; `EDL-1.0` is not an SPDX identifier, and the 2026-11-12 scan below classed the app `blocked` for it. Since then the gate reads `EDL-1.0` as `BSD-3-Clause` (`sdk/tools/applib/licence.py`, `normalise`), and the row now carries the exact SPDX expression from `LICENSE.txt` (issue #199), so the gate confirms the licence as class **L1** (permissive, under the BSD-3-Clause option). The tier and the scan below change only when CI rescans the app (`apps-rescan.yml`); they are never edited by hand.

**Version:** upstream publishes no GitHub releases, only tags. `v2.1.2` is the latest tag (annotated, tagged 2026-02-09; [ChangeLog.txt](https://github.com/eclipse-mosquitto/mosquitto/blob/v2.1.2/ChangeLog.txt) "2.1.2 - 2026-02-09").

**Image:** `docker.io/library/eclipse-mosquitto`, the Docker Official Image built from the upstream [docker/2.1-alpine](https://github.com/eclipse-mosquitto/mosquitto/tree/v2.1.2/docker/2.1-alpine) Dockerfile. For 2.1.2 only the `2.1.2-alpine` tag exists. The index also has arm/v6, 386, ppc64le and s390x images; the manifest declares amd64 and arm64.

**Icon:** a neutral generated icon with initials, not the Eclipse Mosquitto logo.

## How it runs here

- One `Deployment` (`Recreate`, 1 replica) and a `ClusterIP` Service `mosquitto` on port **1883** (MQTT, no TLS). In-cluster clients use `mosquitto.app-mosquitto.svc:1883`.
- **No anonymous access.** The image's default config (`docker/2.1-alpine/mosquitto.conf`) allows anonymous access on 1883 and opens an HTTP dashboard listener on 9883. This package replaces it with the ConfigMap `mosquitto-config` (`manifests/mosquitto.conf`): `allow_anonymous false` and no dashboard listener.
- **Users** come from the [Dynamic Security plugin](https://mosquitto.org/documentation/dynamic-security/). Its config is `/mosquitto/data/dynamic-security.json`. From 2.1, when that file does not exist, the plugin generates it on first start with the users `admin` (administers users and roles) and `democlient` (read/write on `#`), with random passwords stored in plain text in `dynamic-security.json.pw` (see First run).
- **Persistence:** the `persist-sqlite` plugin stores retained messages and persistent sessions in `/mosquitto/data` (upstream [docker README](https://github.com/eclipse-mosquitto/mosquitto/blob/v2.1.2/docker/2.1-alpine/README.md), "Configuration"). Everything lives on the 1 GiB PVC `mosquitto-data`. Logs go to stdout.
- It runs as UID/GID 1883, the `mosquitto` user that the upstream Dockerfile creates, not as root. It also runs with a read-only root filesystem, no privilege escalation, all Linux capabilities dropped and the default seccomp profile. The image has no `USER`: its entrypoint runs as root only to `chown` the data directory. Here, `fsGroup: 1883` gives the process the volume instead.
- Probes: TCP on 1883 for readiness and liveness. MQTT has no HTTP health endpoint.

**Sizing:** upstream publishes no sizing. In the smoke test (k3s, arm64) the broker used about 4 MiB of memory idle, with an 8 MiB peak. Requests are 25m CPU and 32Mi; the 128Mi limit leaves room for many clients and retained messages.

**Smoke test:** the gate's HTTP smoke check does not apply because there is no web port. On a throwaway k3s (Lima, 2026-11-12), these checks passed by hand:
- rollout ready;
- anonymous and wrong-password connections refused (`not authorised`);
- `democlient` published a retained message with the generated password, and it was still delivered after a pod restart;
- `mosquitto_ctrl dynsec` changed the admin password, created a client, deleted `democlient`, and the new client could publish.

## First run

Source: [Dynamic Security plugin, "Generating the configuration file - 2.1 onwards"](https://mosquitto.org/documentation/dynamic-security/) ([source at v2.1.2](https://github.com/eclipse-mosquitto/mosquitto/blob/v2.1.2/www/pages/documentation/dynamic-security.md)), and `man mosquitto_ctrl`.

1. Install Eclipse Mosquitto from the Market and approve the action. It installs into the namespace `app-mosquitto`.
2. Read the generated passwords. The file is plain text, and upstream says to delete it once the passwords are known:
   ```sh
   kubectl -n app-mosquitto exec deploy/mosquitto -- cat /mosquitto/data/dynamic-security.json.pw
   ```
3. Set your own admin password. `mosquitto_ctrl` does not prompt for the password it connects with, so pass the generated admin password with `-P`. It then asks for the new password twice:
   ```sh
   kubectl -n app-mosquitto exec -it deploy/mosquitto -- mosquitto_ctrl -u admin -P '<admin password>' dynsec setClientPassword admin
   ```
4. Create one client per device or app, give it the `client` role (read/write on all application topics), then remove the demo user. Use the new admin password with `-P`; `createClient` asks for the new client's password:
   ```sh
   kubectl -n app-mosquitto exec -it deploy/mosquitto -- mosquitto_ctrl -u admin -P '<admin password>' dynsec createClient zigbee2mqtt
   kubectl -n app-mosquitto exec deploy/mosquitto -- mosquitto_ctrl -u admin -P '<admin password>' dynsec addClientRole zigbee2mqtt client
   kubectl -n app-mosquitto exec deploy/mosquitto -- mosquitto_ctrl -u admin -P '<admin password>' dynsec deleteClient democlient
   ```
   For narrower access, create roles with `mosquitto_ctrl dynsec createRole` and `addRoleACL` (see the same page).
5. Delete the plain-text password file:
   ```sh
   kubectl -n app-mosquitto exec deploy/mosquitto -- rm /mosquitto/data/dynamic-security.json.pw
   ```
6. Point clients at `mosquitto.app-mosquitto.svc:1883` with their username and password. To test from your machine: `kubectl -n app-mosquitto port-forward svc/mosquitto 1883:1883`, then `mosquitto_sub -h localhost -u <user> -P <password> -t '#' -v`.

## Not done yet

- **No TLS listener.** Passwords cross the network in clear text, and `mosquitto_ctrl` warns about it. Keep the broker inside the cluster or home network. TLS (port 8883) needs a certificate, which OneMind does not issue to apps yet.
- **Not reachable from outside the cluster.** Devices on the LAN (ESP32 sensors, for example) need a LoadBalancer or NodePort Service, which this v0 package does not create.
- The upstream HTTP dashboard (port 9883) is not enabled.
- **The bridge needs NATS's MQTT listener, which OneMind's own NATS does not open yet.** The platform NATS runs without an `mqtt {}` block and without JetStream, which NATS's MQTT listener requires (`deploy/systemd/onemind-nats.service`: "Core NATS only ... no JetStream yet"; `deploy/compose/compose.yaml` the same). Until the platform enables both and creates a NATS user for the bridge, leave `nats_mqtt_host` empty (or point it at another NATS server you run). Tracked under FLD-02 (#199).
- MQTT 5 extras (user properties, response topic, content type, message expiry) do not cross the bridge: the NATS leg is MQTT 3.1.1, which has no field for them. Topic, payload and QoS 0/1 do (the round-trip test checks topic and payload).

**Gate status:** this app was held as licence-blocked because the licence-matrix row wrote `EDL-1.0`. The gate now matches the licence (class L1) and passes on amd64 and arm64 (apps-gate-all run 43879258129: pass, verified), so the tier is `verified`. Issue #117.

## Bridge to NATS (MQTT 5 devices on the OneMind bus)

**Why.** OneMind's message bus is NATS. NATS has an MQTT listener, but it accepts only MQTT 3.1.1: its CONNECT handler refuses any protocol level other than 4 with "unacceptable protocol version" ([server/mqtt.go at v2.15.2](https://github.com/nats-io/nats-server/blob/v2.15.2/server/mqtt.go), `mqttProtoLevel`). Many current devices and libraries speak MQTT 5 (level 5), so they cannot join the bus directly. Mosquitto accepts MQTT 5, 3.1.1 and 3.1. Put it in front, and let it forward messages to NATS in 3.1.1, and MQTT 5 devices reach NATS.

**Design: Mosquitto's own bridge, no extra program.** A *bridge* is Mosquitto acting as a client of another broker: it connects out to NATS, and copies messages on chosen topics across ([`mosquitto.conf` man page, "Configuring Bridges"](https://mosquitto.org/man/mosquitto-conf-5.html)). A separate bridge program would be more code to write, test and patch; the built-in bridge is already in the image we ship, maintained upstream, and reconnects on its own when NATS restarts. The settings that matter:

| Bridge setting | Value | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `bridge_protocol_version` | `mqttv311` | the only version NATS accepts |
| `try_private` | `false` | when on, Mosquitto marks its CONNECT as "a bridge" by sending protocol level `0x84`; NATS refuses anything but `4` |
| `topic # out 1 "" mqtt/up/` | always | every device topic `T` is published on NATS as `mqtt/up/T`, which NATS turns into the subject `mqtt.up.T` (slashes become dots: `mqttToNATSSubjectConversion` in the same file) |
| `topic # in 1 "" mqtt/down/` | only with `nats_bridge_down` | NATS messages on `mqtt.down.T` arrive at devices as `T` |
| `notifications` | `false` | no Mosquitto-internal `$SYS/broker/connection/...` messages on the bus |
| `remote_clientid` | `onemind-mosquitto-bridge` | one stable session on NATS |

Two separate prefixes (`up` and `down`) mean the bridge never subscribes to its own output, so messages cannot loop. On top of that, Mosquitto's bridge subscribes locally with MQTT's "no local" option ([src/bridge.c at v2.1.2](https://github.com/eclipse-mosquitto/mosquitto/blob/v2.1.2/src/bridge.c)), so a message that came in over the bridge is not sent back. Bridge connections are exempt from the Dynamic Security access lists ([src/plugin_acl_check.c at v2.1.2](https://github.com/eclipse-mosquitto/mosquitto/blob/v2.1.2/src/plugin_acl_check.c)), so no extra Mosquitto user is needed for it.

**Devices to NATS only, by default.** Data flowing up (sensor readings) is safe to copy. The down direction lets anything that can publish on NATS under `mqtt.down.>` send commands to devices, so it is off until the owner turns on `nats_bridge_down`. OneMind's rule is that AI never actuates without human approval: changing that setting is an app-settings action that goes through the gateway's approval flow, and NATS permissions for `mqtt.down.>` should be granted only to the gateway's approved-action path, never to an agent directly.

**How it is configured.** Mosquitto's config file cannot read environment variables, so the container starts `manifests/start.sh` (shipped in the `mosquitto-config` ConfigMap) instead of the image's entrypoint. The script copies `mosquitto.conf`, appends the bridge block built from the app's settings, and starts Mosquitto. Every value is checked first (host: letters, digits, `.` and `-`; port 1-65535; no spaces or line breaks in the user name or password), because Mosquitto's config format has no quoting: a value with a line break could otherwise add its own config lines, for example `allow_anonymous true`.

| Setting (Market, ConfigMap `onemind-settings`) | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `nats_mqtt_host` | empty | NATS MQTT listener host; empty means no bridge |
| `nats_mqtt_port` | `1883` | its port |
| `nats_mqtt_username` | empty | NATS user the bridge logs in as |
| `nats_bridge_down` | `false` | also deliver NATS `mqtt.down.>` to devices |

The NATS password is a secret, not a setting (settings are written to the audit log). It is declared under `spec.secrets` as `mosquitto-nats-bridge` / `NATS_MQTT_PASSWORD`; the owner enters it, and the gateway creates the Secret, so no password is in this repository. The runtime config holding it is written with mode `0600` to an in-memory volume (`emptyDir`, `medium: Memory`), never to the data disk, and the script never logs it.

**Test.** `apps/mosquitto/tests/test_bridge.py` checks the generated config (bridge off without a host, the bridge lines, and refusal of every value that could inject config), then starts the pinned NATS 2.15.3 and Mosquitto 2.1.2 images in Docker the way the app runs (start.sh as the command, UID 1883, read-only root filesystem). It proves both halves of the story: an MQTT 5 client is refused by NATS directly, and the same MQTT 5 client round-trips a message: it publishes `sensors/kitchen/temp` to Mosquitto, a NATS client receives it on `mqtt.up.sensors.kitchen.temp` and answers on `mqtt.down.commands.kitchen.fan`, and the MQTT 5 client receives `commands/kitchen/fan`, with no copy looping back to NATS. CI runs it in `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, job `mqtt-bridge`; locally: `python3 -I -m unittest discover -s apps/mosquitto/tests -v` (the Docker part is skipped without Docker).
